items.followUp: State two differences between prokaryotic cells and eukaryotic cells.

rubric.why: Identifies somatic cells as ordinary body cells.
rubric.description: Somatic cells are body cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying somatic cells as body cells.

rubric.why: Distinguishes germ line cells by their role in producing gametes.
rubric.description: Germ line cells give rise to gametes; somatic cells do not.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that germ line cells produce gametes, in contrast to somatic cells.

modelAnswer: Somatic cells are the ordinary body cells; germ line cells are cells that give rise to gametes.
Somatic cells are not involved in producing gametes, whereas germ line cells produce them.

items.followUp: What is the Calvin cycle, and where does it occur in a chloroplast?

rubric.why: Identifies dark reactions as light-independent reactions.
rubric.description: Dark reactions do not directly require light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that dark reactions are light-independent.

rubric.why: Identifies the chloroplast stroma and carbon dioxide fixation as central features.
rubric.description: They occur in the stroma and use carbon dioxide to form carbohydrates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the site and role in carbohydrate formation.

modelAnswer: Dark reactions are the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis; they do not directly require light.
They occur in the stroma of the chloroplast, where carbon dioxide is used to form carbohydrates using ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.

rubric.why: Describes the active site as a particular region of an enzyme.
rubric.description: The active site is a specific region or pocket of an enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the active site as a specific region of the enzyme.

rubric.why: Explains substrate binding and the role of the site in catalysis.
rubric.description: The substrate binds at the active site, where the reaction is catalysed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking substrate binding at the active site with catalysis.

modelAnswer: The active site is a specific region or pocket of an enzyme to which its substrate binds.
The enzyme and substrate form an enzyme-substrate complex at this site, where the reaction is catalysed.

items.followUp: Define an enzyme and state what it acts upon.

rubric.why: Defines substrates as substances that enzymes act upon.
rubric.description: Substrates are the substances or reactants on which enzymes act.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining substrates as substances or reactants acted upon by enzymes.

rubric.why: Adds how substrates interact with enzymes or what happens to them.
rubric.description: A substrate binds to an enzyme's active site and is converted into product(s).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate binds to the active site or is converted into products.

modelAnswer: Substrates are the substances or reactants on which enzymes act.
A substrate binds to an enzyme's active site and is converted into product(s).

rubric.why: Identifies a cofactor as a non-protein component associated with an enzyme.
rubric.description: A cofactor is a non-protein component required by an enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a cofactor is a non-protein component of an enzyme.

rubric.why: States the cofactor's necessity for enzyme function or gives a valid type.
rubric.description: It is required for enzyme activity and may be an inorganic ion or an organic molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is needed for enzyme activity or giving a valid type.

modelAnswer: A cofactor is a non-protein component associated with an enzyme.
It is required for the enzyme's activity and may be an inorganic ion or an organic molecule.

items.followUp: Describe the cellular and organ levels of organization in a living organism.

rubric.why: Explains that atoms join to form molecules at the molecular level.
rubric.description: Atoms combine to form molecules at the molecular level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the formation of molecules from atoms.

rubric.why: Shows how molecules contribute to larger cell structures.
rubric.description: Molecules form or contribute to cell structures such as organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking molecules to organelles or cell structures.

rubric.why: Defines a tissue as a group of similar cells.
rubric.description: A tissue is a group of similar cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining tissue as a group of similar cells.

rubric.why: States the shared function of cells within a tissue.
rubric.description: The cells of a tissue work together to perform a particular function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that tissue cells perform a common function.

modelAnswer: At the molecular level, atoms combine through chemical bonds to form molecules such as water, proteins and DNA.
Molecules form or contribute to cell structures, including organelles.
At the tissue level, a group of similar cells forms a tissue.
The cells in a tissue work together to perform a particular function.

items.followUp: Give two reasons why viruses are considered non-living and two reasons why they show characteristics of living things.

rubric.why: Notes the absence of cellular organization in viruses.
rubric.description: Viruses are acellular and have no cellular structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viruses lack cellular structure.

rubric.why: Gives a non-living feature of viruses outside a host.
rubric.description: Outside a host, viruses are inactive and cannot reproduce; they can be crystallized.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid non-living feature.

rubric.why: Recognizes reproduction inside a living host cell as a living characteristic.
rubric.description: Inside a living host cell, viruses can reproduce.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viruses reproduce inside host cells.

rubric.why: Concludes that viruses lie at the boundary of living and non-living or supplies a relevant structural feature.
rubric.description: Because of these contrasting features, viruses are regarded as being at the boundary of living and non-living things.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the boundary conclusion or a relevant feature such as nucleic acid enclosed in a protein coat.

modelAnswer: Viruses are acellular and have no cellular structure or independent metabolism.
Outside a host cell, they are inactive and cannot reproduce; they can even be crystallized.
Inside a living host cell, viruses reproduce and show some characteristics of living things.
Therefore, viruses are regarded as lying at the boundary between living and non-living things.

items.followUp: Describe the main events of the Calvin cycle and name the products it uses from the light reactions.

rubric.why: Defines light reactions as the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Light reactions are the reactions of photosynthesis that require light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Identifies the site of light reactions in the chloroplast.
rubric.description: They occur on the thylakoid membranes, particularly in the grana.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct site.

rubric.why: Describes light absorption by chlorophyll.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll absorbs light.

rubric.why: Includes splitting of water and oxygen release.
rubric.description: Water is split, releasing oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing water splitting and oxygen release.

rubric.why: States the formation of energy and reducing-power products used in dark reactions.
rubric.description: ATP and NADPH are formed during the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming ATP and NADPH as products.

modelAnswer: Light reactions are the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis, occurring in the presence of light.
They take place on the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast, especially in the grana.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and the excited electrons pass through an electron transport system.
Water is split (photolysis), releasing oxygen and supplying hydrogen and electrons.
Light energy is used to make ATP, and NADP is reduced to NADPH; ATP and NADPH are used in the dark reactions.
